 Featured Commentary 
 Bill Johnston-Walsh: On Social Security, older Pennsylvanians need more than an adjustment
 By Bill Johnston-Walsh 3 Min Read 
 • Nov. 13, 2026 
 | 2 minutes ago 
-->
 Go Ad-Free today 
 The East Liberty Social Security Administration office is seen June 19. (Justin Vellucci | TribLive) 
 For millions of Pennsylvanians, the annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is more than a number. It’s a lifeline for paying rent, buying groceries, home repairs and car payments. And for too many residents here in the commonwealth, their monthly payment isn’t keeping up with the increasing cost of living in 2026.
 The federal government recently announced a 3.6% Social Security COLA, which, for the average Social Security recipient, means an additional $900 per year. Much of that news got lost with the recent midterm elections, but it’s worth remembering that while the COLA helps, for too many older Americans, it is not keeping pace with the rising costs of everyday life.
 A recent AARP survey of older adults found most adults age 50-plus (76%) say the COLA increase in 2027 does not seem like it is keeping up with rising prices — attitudes that have remained consistent in recent years.
 Across Pennsylvania, people tell us they are feeling the pressure. Groceries cost more. Utility bills consume a larger share of monthly budgets. Healthcare and prescription drug costs continue to strain families. For someone living on a fixed income, even a modest increase in costs can force difficult choices that reverberate through our economy. 
 One in five Pennsylvanians — over 3 million residents — receive a Social Security payment. The average payment is $2,142 monthly or $25,707 annually. These payments inject $71.8 billion into the state’s economy every year. 
 Social Security recipients paid into it with every paycheck. They earned it through decades of hard work. This money belongs to them, and they depend on it. 
 Half of Social Security recipients say it is their main source of income, and most Americans 50-plus say the 2027 COLA increase will not keep up with rising prices, according to AARP research. That means even with an adjustment, too many older Americans still feel like they’re falling behind. 
 Yet special interests in Washington, D.C., continue to push ideas that would reduce or cut the COLA. These proposals are out of touch with the reality facing older Americans in communities across our state. 
 This year’s COLA matters because every dollar matters. But protecting Americans from rising prices requires more than an annual adjustment. It requires protecting and strengthening the Social Security benefits Americans have earned.
 Congress must act to ensure Social Security is there for today’s retirees and for the generations still paying into it with every paycheck, without cutting the money they have earned.
 Pennsylvania’s message is simple: Keep the promise. Protect and strengthen Social Security for the Americans who earned it. 
 Bill Johnston-Walsh is the state director of AARP Pennsylvania.
